items.title: Is jouw bibliotheek goed verzekerd? Dat weet je pas als je het controleert
items.raw_text: Deze inhoud is beschermd met een wachtwoord. Voer hieronder je wachtwoord in om het te bekijken. Wachtwoord:

items.title: Zó schrijf je een goede contentstrategie
items.raw_text: Alle bibliotheken hebben vaak dezelfde uitdaging; ze hebben enorm veel te vertellen over wat er bij hen te doen en beleven is. Het liefst deel je deze communicatie op zo veel mogelijk kanalen met een zo groot mogelijk bereik. Maar komt deze informatie wel aan? En bij wie? Hoe meer focus je aanbrengt, hoe beter je boodschap blijft hangen bij jouw doelgroep. Een goede contentstrategie vormt hierbij de basis. Bij contentmarketing draait het om keuzes maken. Keuzes maken in wie je wilt bereiken, wat je wilt vertellen, in welke vorm en wanneer. Dat betekent in het geval van bibliotheken vooral keuzes maken in wat je niet meer doet. Dat is lastig, maar gaat je uiteindelijk helpen om meer focus aan te brengen en meer impact te verkrijgen. Hoe gerichter en relevanter jouw content, hoe beter deze ook aankomt bij jouw doelgroep(en). Op die manier val je mensen niet ‘lastig’ met content die voor hen niet interessant is en het dus voelt als een information overload . In lijn met beleidsplan Keuzes maak je niet op basis van je contentaanbod, maar op basis van je strategie. De keuzes die jij dus voor je content maakt, vloeien o.a. voort uit het beleidsplan van jouw bibliotheek. Het ligt dus in lijn met de rest waar jouw bibliotheek mee bezig is. Zoals je in onderstaande piramide ziet, is het maken van content pas het laatste waar je mee aan slag gaat, eerst moet de basis goed staan. items.title: Digitaal burgerschap: verleden, heden en toekomst
items.raw_text: Van ‘digitaal burgerschap’ bestaan geen vergeelde foto’s in een oude schoenendoos . Je kunt eigenlijk niet echt zeggen : “ I k weet nog toen…”. Toch heeft digitaal burgerschap inmiddels een geschiedenis. In een paar jaar tijd hebben we verkend, geëxperimenteerd en geleerd . Stap voor stap werd duidelijker wat digitaal burgerschap voor bibliotheken betekent . Daarmee is er inmiddels een verleden, heden én een toekomst . Een mooi moment om terug te kijken op waar we vandaan komen, stil te staan bij waar we nu zijn en vooruit te kijken naar wat er nog voor ons ligt. Kijk je mee? Toen: 5 jaar geleden De term digitaal burgerschap werd voor het eerst in de branche geïntroduceerd. We begonnen de term in onze branche te laten landen. Het werd spreekwoordelijk ‘de boer op’ met digitaal burgerschap: wat is het, waarom is het belangrijk, en wat kan en moet de bibliotheek ermee? Er ontstond direct al een zoektocht naar verschillende mogelijkheden, uitkomsten, meningen en perspectieven. Te midden van technologische ontwikkelingen als de opkomst van generatieve AI, filterbubbels en podcasts voor iedereen, werd digitaal burgerschap geboren. Duidelijk was dat er een gezamenlijke taal nodig was, om vast te stellen wat digitaal burgerschap precies is hoe het past/raakt aan de dienstverlening van de bibliotheek. items.title: Wat gebeurt er als onze afgeschreven boeken grondstof worden voor AI?
items.raw_text: Anthropic, een Amerikaans bedrijf dat zich bezighoudt met kunstmatige intelligentie, haalde begin 2024 de voormalige architect van Google’s boekenscanprogramma binnen, met als opdracht alle boeken ter wereld te verwerven. Intern kreeg dat de codenaam Panama, volgens de eigen planningsdocumenten omdat men liever niet had dat bekend werd waar het bedrijf mee bezig was. De omschrijving in datzelfde stuk laat weinig aan de verbeelding over: het destructief scannen van alle boeken ter wereld. Wil je liever naar de column luisteren? Beluister dan onderstaande podcastaflevering. In een reeks columns over AI neemt Erik Reuvers, adviseur Digitale Geletterdheid bij Probiblio je mee in de wereld van artificiële intelligentie en wat die betekent voor bibliotheken. Niet alleen technisch, maar juist vanuit de waarden waar bibliotheken voor staan. Wat volgde ligt inmiddels vast in rechtbankstukken. Miljoenen tweedehands boeken werden opgekocht, de ruggen er met hydraulische snijders afgehaald, de pagina’s door snelscanners gehaald en de resten weggegooid. Een Amerikaanse rechter oordeelde in juni 2025 dat dit onder fair use viel, juist omdat het origineel werd vernietigd en er dus geen tweede exemplaar ontstond. Sindsdien is er een markt ontstaan. Tweedehandsboekverkopers krijgen bulkorders van soms een miljoen exemplaren, waarbij tussenpartijen aanbieden de identiteit van de koper geheim te houden. Gezocht wordt vooral naar werk van voor 2022, want dat bevat gegarandeerd geen machinetekst.

Een andere manier van werken, wat voor bibliotheken best even wennen kan zijn. Maar hoe kies en prioriteer je welke content het belangrijkst is? Het 3H-model helpt hierbij. Als marketing-/communicatieteam ga je zo veel gerichter en relevanter communiceren en werk je als team steeds meer proactief in plaats van reactief. Zoals je in onderstaande afbeelding kunt zien, bestaat het model uit drie lagen: een bovenste laag ‘hero’s’, in het midden de ‘hubs’ en een onderste brede laag ‘hygiëne’. Zoals je in het model kunt zien, kies je er maximaal drie. Dit komt doordat je veel aandacht, geld en middelen besteedt aan deze onderwerpen en ze echt in de spotlight zet. items.title: Online Taalhuis: kansen, uitdagingen en praktijk
items.raw_text: Online taalactiviteiten maken taalondersteuning toegankelijker voor mensen die niet altijd naar de bibliotheek kunnen komen of overdag niet beschikbaar zijn. Steeds meer bibliotheken breiden hun fysieke a anbod uit met online taalactiviteiten . We organiseerden een Summerschool over dit onderwerp, en daarom verzamelde ik praktische inzichten hierover. Ik ging in gesprek met Paula Sangers, senior medewerker Basisvaardigheden en coördinator van een online Taalcafé van Bibliotheek Zuid-Hollandse Eilanden. In dit artikel lees je de kansen, uitdagingen en aandachtspunten van online taalactiviteiten . Voordelen van online taalactiviteit en Een online aanbod maakt het mogelijk om doelgroepen te bereiken die anders moeilijk deelnemen aan activiteiten van het Taalhuis. Daarbij kan je denken aan bv. intakegesprek, Taalcafe,taalcoaching, leesclub, ezv. Voor mensen die overdag werken, ouders met jonge kinderen of inwoners die verder van de bibliotheek wonen, biedt een online Taalhuis vaak de flexibiliteit die nodig is om toch mee te doen. Ook voor mantelzorgers, mensen met gezondheidsproblemen of een beperkte mobiliteit kan online deelname een uitkomst zijn. Een ander voordeel is dat zowel deelnemers als begeleiders kunnen aansluiten vanuit huis, onderweg of vanaf een andere locatie. Op deze manier kunnen de taalleerders in contact met de taal blijven ook vanuit buitenland. De deelname wordt minder afhankelijk van reistijd, vakanties en bereikbaarheid. items.title: Visietraject bij MFCO Rozet: de kunst van impactgericht werken
items.raw_text: Ga je een verandertraject altijd in omdat iets niet goed gaat? Nee, blijkt uit het verhaal van Rozet. Bij deze Arnhemse multifunctionele culturele organisatie (MFCO) zaten de adviseurs Taal en Cultuur behoorlijk op een lijn. De samenwerking binnen team Educatie verliep organisch en intuïtief. Toch was er behoefte aan ondersteuning bij een gezamenlijke visie. Ook wilde het team antwoord op de vraag ‘doen we de juiste dingen en hebben die de juiste impact?’ Daar kwam Rijnbrink in beeld. En welke adviezen hebben ze voor andere bibliotheken en MFCO’s? De kracht van verbinding Nataschenka en Roos zijn sinds kort teamleider van team Educatie bij Rozet. Die diversiteit is illustratief voor de manier van werken en de visie van Rozet. ‘Als adviseurs gaan we met basisscholen in gesprek over de hele breedte van taal, kunst en erfgoed’, vertelt Nataschenka. ‘Vanuit hun behoeften organiseren we verschillende projecten en samenwerkingen. items.title: Schuren mag! 7x inzichten over democratie en burgerschap
items.raw_text: Een literaire avond in je bibliotheek over een onderwerp dat gevoelig ligt. Een school die een collectie afwijst vanwege levensovertuigingen. Of een gesprek tussen mensen die lijnrecht tegenover elkaar staan… Als bibliotheek ben je er voor iedereen. Maar kun je er eigenlijk wel voor iedereen zijn? En hoe ga je om met meningen die botsen met elkaar, of misschien zelfs met die van jou? Op 24 september gingen zo’n 350 bibliotheekprofessionals hierover met elkaar in gesprek tijdens het Kennisfestival Democratie & Burgerschap , georganiseerd door SPN . Een uitspraak die gedurende de dag vaak terugkwam: ‘Schuren mag.’ Onze Rijnbrink-collega’s waren erbij en keerden huiswaarts met nieuwe inzichten, praktische tips en stof tot nadenken. In dit artikel delen we de belangrijkste inzichten van de dag. Als bibliotheek heb je een belangrijke rol in het versterken van democratie en burgerschap. Die opdracht staat ook beschreven in het Bibliotheekconvenant 2024-2027 . Democratie is niet vanzelfsprekend. Het vraagt om aandacht, oefening en soms ook moed. Willeke Slingerland is lector Sociale Cohesie en de Democratische Rechtsstaat aan de Hogeschool Utrecht. Zij stelt: ‘Bibliotheken zijn de kanaries, oftewel waakhonden, van de democratie. items.title: AI-vermeldingen, CAPTCHA en meer: praktische tips voor privacy en informatiebeveiliging
items.raw_text: Privacy en informatiebeveiliging blijven actuele onderwerpen voor bibliotheken. Sinds 2 augustus is het bijvoorbeeld verplicht om transparant te zijn over gebruik van AI. Om jullie zo goed mogelijk op de hoogte te houden, delen we iedere twee maanden het laatste nieuws, ontwikkelingen, praktische tips en opleidingsmogelijkheden op het gebied van privacy en informatiebeveiliging. items.title: Maak kennis met Constance: de kracht achter de onderwijscollecties
items.raw_text: Tussen de boekenkasten in het collectiegebouw van Rijnbrink werkt Constance Melissen. Als collectiebeheerder Onderwijs zorgt zij ervoor dat scholen boeken krijgen die aansluiten bij hun lessen én de leefwereld van kinderen en jongeren. Zo draagt ze bij aan leesplezier bij de jeugd. In dit artikel maak je kennis met Constance en het werk dat zij doet. Wie regelmatig op een basisschool komt, herkent het meteen: de themahoek. Vaak vol met boeken in een bepaald thema. Soms door de leerkracht aangevuld met accessoires. Een thema is bijvoorbeeld kerst, of vervoer. Maar ook duurzaamheid of sprookjes. Bij Rijnbrink noemen we dit onderwijscollecties. De boeken zijn verzameld rondom een thema. Ze sluiten aan bij de leefwereld van kinderen en passen bij het niveau van verschillende leeftijdsgroepen in het basisonderwijs en de kinderopvang. Zo ontdekken kinderen nieuwe onderwerpen en lezen ze boeken die aansluiten bij hun interesses en ontwikkeling. Ook helpt het de leraren bij het geven van hun lessen. Scholen kunnen zelf online een themacollectie bestellen en deze zes weken lenen. Werken tussen de boeken Constance is verantwoordelijk voor de onderwijscollecties. Zij bepaalt welke boeken bij een thema passen. En zorgt ervoor dat het pakket met themaboeken bij de scholen komen. Haar werk doet ze letterlijk tussen de boeken. items.title: Frisse financiële start in 2027? 5x tips voor jouw jaarafsluiting

items.title: Op weg naar slimmer en duurzamer transport
items.raw_text: We merken het allemaal aan de pomp: de prijs van brandstof is hoog. Maandelijks betaalt Rijnbrink nu €3.000 meer aan brandstof dan een jaar geleden. Het is daarom noodzakelijk om efficiënt en duurzaam te rijden. Misschien merk je dat als bibliotheek of school, omdat we materialen op een andere tijd bezorgen dan je gewend bent. In dit artikel vertellen collega’s Hans Bender en Daan Meijer van Facilitair & Logistiek over hoe zij werken aan efficiënt en toekomstbestendig transport. Waar willen zij naartoe? items.title: Groeien in je rol als vrijwilligerscoördinator, hoe doe je dat?

items.title: Prinsjesdag 2026: 5 thema’s uitgelicht voor bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Prinsjesdag 2026 zit erop. De nieuw gepresenteerde plannen laten zien dat het kabinet vertrouwen heeft in de toekomst van bibliotheken. Er komt meer zekerheid voor leesbevordering, bibliotheken krijgen een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol en er is geld voor verdere ontwikkeling. Tegelijkertijd zijn er ook uitdagingen. Gaby Erckens, onze teamleider Financiën en Control, dook in de plannen en zette de belangrijkste 5 thema’s op een rij. 1. Structureel geld voor leesbevordering Goed nieuws is dat de programma’s BoekStart en de Bibliotheek op school vanaf 2027 structurele financiering krijgen. items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. Hun verhaal begint bij taalmodellen, maar raakt al snel aan een veel fundamentelere vraag: hoe houdt de overheid zelf regie over haar digitale toekomst? Binnen de Nederlandse Digitaliseringsstrategie is AI daarom een prioriteit: de overheid wil AI verantwoord inzetten voor maatschappelijke opgaven en betere dienstverlening, succesvolle toepassin

items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. Geopolitieke spanningen, conflicterende rechtsstelsels, concentratie van leveranciersmacht en complexe beheerketens maken zichtbaar dat organisaties niet langer kunnen volstaan met contracten, certificaten of algemene toezeggingen. items.title: Learning by Doing: IFLA Futures Club #5
items.raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. items.title: Open science opens the process, not just the paper
items.raw_text: Beyond open access There is no doubt that open access has made major progress: about half of all papers are now published open access worldwide. However, making a paper readable is only the first step and “readable in the sense of open access doesn’t mean reliable or ready for replication,” remarked Prof. Robin Wilkening in the October 6th, 2026 webinar Beyond Open Access: Open Science Across the Entire Research Cycle , co-hosted by the Science and Technology Libraries Section and the Advisory Committee on Open Science and Scholarship . A scientific paper is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it are the research question, hypothesis, methods, protocols, instruments, data, code, and reviews that make the research possible. If these remain inaccessible, researchers are simply unable to replicate published findings. Wilkening, therefore, argues for open science across the entire research cycle, rather than focusing only on the final publication. Opening the research cycle Openness can begin with funding and continue through study design, data collection, analysis, publication, evaluation, and reuse. Researchers can pre-register their hypotheses and analysis plans, make instruments and tools open, deposit data and code in repositories, and use preprints to make findings available for discussion before the journal publication process is complete. items.title: IFLA at 100: Looking Back on the ARL Blog
items.raw_text: Mimi Calter, Chair The IFLA Academic & Research Libraries Section is very happy to have you as a reader of our blog! The section has had a blog since 2012, typically posting twice a month, and in that time we’ve been able to publish some remarkable pieces. We are very proud of the history represented in those years of publishing. Unfortunately, much of that history is no longer easily linkable. In 2025, for administrative reasons, we had to retire the WordPress platform that we had been using and transition to the IFLA website as our host site. All of our old posts are preserved, in multiple formats, and are publicly accessible through the IFLA repository (URI: https://repository.ifla.org/handle/20.500.14598/7439 ). However, we no longer have a way to link readers directly to those older posts. To address this issue, and in the spirit of celebrating 100 years of IFLA, we will be introducing a “Looking Back” feature to our blog. We will republish some of our most noteworthy blog posts from the past, sometimes with an update if there is new news to share. The Looking Back posts will be an addition to our ongoing blog postings. If you have a favorite post from the past, let us know! We’ll be happy to add that content to the Looking Back series. And we hope you enjoy looking back and forward!

items.title: Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25
items.raw_text: Australians are using their public libraries in growing numbers, with visits, borrowing and participation in library programs continuing to rise despite increasing pressure on funding and staffing. The Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25 , released by the Australian Library and Information Association (ALIA) and National and State Libraries Australasia (NSLA), provides a national snapshot of public library services and how Australians are using them. The figures tell a good news story, with Australian communities increasingly turning to their public libraries for collections, spaces, online services, programs and activities. Physical and online library visits increased by 8.5% in a single year, reaching a five-year high of more than 160 million visits. Public library collections were used almost 180 million times, while a record 434,000 library programs attracted more than 7.2 million attendees. Digital engagement also continues to grow, with digital collection use increasing by 80% over five years and Wi-Fi use almost doubling since 2021–22. Libraries are increasingly being used as places to meet, work and connect, with meeting-room use up 24% in the past year and 81% since 2021–22. Despite the steady increase in usage, public libraries are meeting this heightened demand within an increasingly constrained funding environment. items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. American Libraries spoke with five authors on the Top 11 Most Challenged Books of 2025 list included in the report to hear how their experiences affected them. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.raw_text: Buffeted by Change, Researchers Seek Continuity and Investment: Results from the Ithaka S+R US Researcher Survey was written by: Chelsea McCracken Dylan Ruediger Ruby MacDougall From the Report’s Executive Summary: The research enterprise in the United States, established after the second world war, is experiencing massive disruption. US colleges and universities are grappling with federal and state disinvestment and intervention at a time when AI and other technologies are reshaping how research is conducted and its findings are communicated. As a result, researchers at US higher education institutions are operating in an unstable environment. Against this backdrop, the findings from our survey of 4,003 researchers, fielded in late 2025, demonstrate that they remain committed to carrying out essential work and that they are doing so in innovative ways—through collaboration, the creation of valuable educational experiences, and pushing knowledge towards the next frontier. While researchers don’t necessarily agree on how their sector should respond to the changing environment, our findings underscore the importance of stability, continuity, and sustained investment. items.raw_text: From Nature: Elena Vasquez spent three months camping on the rim of Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of the Congo back in 2019. She says the sulfur dioxide there smelt like “burnt matches mixed with rotten eggs”. Her colleague, Marcus Chen, has witnessed 11 volcanic eruptions across four continents. Vasquez and Chen’s accounts appeared on Volcanoes Explored, a now-defunct website that described itself as a resource for “exploring the dynamic world of volcanoes”. But there’s a problem: these tales are not real and the pair of volcanology specialists is made up. Vasquez and Chen are ‘ghost’ identities generated by Claude — the large language model (LLM) made by Anthropic in San Francisco — when prompted by users to create fictional experts, according to a preprint published in June. Gemini, Google’s LLM, was found to use a different pair of recurring characters, called Aris Thorne and Lena Petrova, and OpenAI’s GPT repeatedly used the name Elara Voss. [Clip] Fake experts such as these can be found across the Internet as everything from blockchain specialists and astronauts to board members and podcast hosts, and they raise specific concerns around integrity of the scientific literature, say Neo Christopher Chung and Michał Brzozowski, computer scientists at the Samsung AI Center Warsaw in Poland and co-authors of the preprint. items.title: Mellon Foundation Releases: “Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives” Report
items.raw_text: From the Mellon Foundation: Today, the Mellon Foundation released “Powerful but Precarious: Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives,” the first national study of its kind. Produced in partnership with research firm Engage R+D, the study draws on a survey of 336 independent, community-led archives, and in-depth interviews with more than 20 practitioners across the country. Community-based archives are independent organizations that collect and preserve the records, photographs, oral histories, personal papers, and other artifacts of communities many of which have been historically excluded from mainstream institutions. Unlike institutional archives, community-based archives often hold materials that exist nowhere else – collections that, if lost, cannot be recovered. Additionally, community-based archives often operate outside of the context of universities, libraries, historical societies, or other collecting institutions and in doing so, they serve as civic infrastructure where people can access and learn about their own localized or underexplored histories. While hundreds of these archives exist across the United States, serving communities of every background and geography, they have never been mapped, counted, or examined at this scale—leaving them largely invisible to the funders, policymakers, and organizations best positioned to support them. items.raw_text: From Nature: A new Chinese-owned journal has set its sights on rivalling the world’s oldest and most influential academic titles. Vita is one of several English-language journals that have launched in China in the past couple of years. They represent the country’s latest effort to create prestigious global journals, as part of the government’s Journal Excellence Action Plan, which began in 2019. [Clip] Vita is jointly funded by the Higher Education Press, a subsidiary of China’s Ministry of Education based in Beijing, and Westlake University in Hangzhou, its editorial team says. It publishes papers in biological sciences. Its first print issue came out in July. As an open-access journal, Vita waives article-processing charges (APCs), fees many publishers require authors to pay when publishing open access articles. [Clip] Vita ’s model is “clearly going to be appealing” to authors, says James Butcher, a former publisher who runs a consultancy firm called Journalology near Liverpool, UK. But he warns that keeping the model running in the long term will be a challenge for the journal and its funders because “publishing is expensive”. Publishers who charge APCs say that the money helps to cover the costs of publishing open access, including paying the salaries of in-house editors and production staff, as well as printing and server costs. items.title: Report: Oxford Lets OpenAI Train Its AI Models On Historical Texts From the Bodleian Library
items.raw_text: From The Guardian: The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data. The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents. Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers. However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data. [Clip] Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. DeAndra Davis’s The Lovers, The Liars, And Me is a tender coming-of-age story that sensitively handles estrangement, coming out, cultural identity, and the complicated feelings that arise when you enter the adult world. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Connections, Ideas, and a Little Hope: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I had the distinct honor of attending PLA 2026 in Minneapolis thanks to a PLA scholarship. As an eastern North Dakota native, Minneapolis is a familiar destination, but spending several days surrounded by thousands of energized library professionals made the city feel vibrant and new, despite the wind, cold, snow, and more wind. The connections, reunions, and conversations I experienced throughout the conference reminded me why gatherings like PLA matter. Alongside reconnecting with colleagues and making new professional connections, I left with fresh ideas, practical tools, and renewed optimism about the future of libraries. Several sessions stood out to me, both because of their content and because of the presenters who brought those ideas to life. One of the first sessions I attended was “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” presented by Mary Kapusta of Calgary Public Library. Kapusta was engaging, funny, honest, and refreshingly candid about both the successes and challenges of implementing a completely redesigned internal communications strategy across 23 library branches. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. Calgary Public Library serves nearly 1,000 employees, while my library employs roughly 30 staff members, yet many of the concepts felt immediately applicable. items.title: What I Wrote in the Margins of My Notebook: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I arrived at my first Public Library Association Conference expecting to leave with organized notes, a clear list of takeaways, and practical ideas to share with colleagues. Instead, I left with a notebook full of starred ideas, half-written thoughts, and questions scribbled in the margins. Looking back, those messy notes reveal the sessions that stayed with me long after the conference ended. Conversations about internal communication, programming for older adults, and flexible, community-centered services challenged my assumptions and sparked new ideas for my own work. Sessions including “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” “Aging Together: Library Programming for Older Adults,” and “Memory Cafes in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections” reframed how I think about serving both staff and patrons. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content.
